rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence explains “we never heard of this” and sums up the chiefs’ preceding exhortation to persist with their gods.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو المتحصل من كلامهم المبدوء ب { امشوا واصبروا على ءالهتكم } فهذه الجملة كالفذلكة لكلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhtilāq is fabricated falsehood for which its speaker has no plausible grounds.
rows.anchor: والاختلاق : الكذب المخترع الذي لا شبهة لقائله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may continue the general disbelievers’ speech: it connects to 38:5 and explains “liar” in 38:4 as a second predicate; the intervening chiefs’ speech is parenthetical.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون { أءنزل عليه الذكر من بيننا } من كلام عموم الكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, this is the chiefs’ own speech; their utterance makes the other disbelievers’ assent to the charge of lying clear, so no separate explanation is needed.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون من تمام كلام الملأ واستغني به عن بيان جملة { كذاب }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial targets the circumstantial phrase “among us”: they resent Muhammad’s selection, as in 43:31, while the context shows their deeper rejection of messengerhood itself.
rows.anchor: والاستفهام إنكاري ، ومناط الإنكار هو الظرف { من بيننا }

words: بَلْ هُم فِى شَكٍّ مِّن ذِكْرِى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes this a rebuttal: their real doubt is whether God sends anyone as a messenger; “doubt” can figuratively denote certainty, as in 6:33.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون هذا جوابا عن قولهم : { أءنزل عليه الذكر من بيننا }

words: بَلْ هُم فِى شَكٍّ مِّن ذِكْرِى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “rather” begins a new report: they genuinely doubt what the Qur’an is, alternately calling it invented, poetry, magic, ancient tales, or soothsaying.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون انتقالا من خبر عنهم إلى خبر آخر فيكون استئنافا وتكون { بل } للإضراب الانتقالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “My Reminder” is attributed to God to honor it and establish its divine origin; the explicit noun repeats “the Reminder” to underscore that honor.
rows.anchor: وإضافة الذكر إلى ضمير المتكلم وهو الله تعالى إضافة تشريف ولتحقيق كونه من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mīʿād is a verbal noun of place or time in form, used here with the meaning “promise.”
rows.anchor: والميعاد : مصدر ميمي بمعنى الوعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain and growth passage begins the sūra’s Qur’an-and-Islam guidance theme, resumed in 39:22–23 after the excursus beginning at 39:2.
rows.anchor: استئناف ابتدائي انتقل به إلى غرض التنويه بالقرآن وما احتوى عليه من هدى الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain sent down from heaven represents the Qur’an’s descent, which revives hearts.
rows.anchor: فإنزال الماء من السماء تشبيه لإنزال القرآن لإحياء القلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water channeled into underground springs represents the Qur’an being conveyed to people.
rows.anchor: وإسلاك الماء ينابيع في الأرض تشبيه لتبليغ القرآن للناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Crops of varied colors represent people differing as good or bad, beneficial or harmful.
rows.anchor: وإخراج الزرع المختلف الألوان تشبيه لحال اختلاف الناس من طيب وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flourishing crop represents believers multiplying among the polytheists.
rows.anchor: وهياج الزرع تشبيه لتكاثر المؤمنين بين المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The crop becoming dry debris also recalls death, in which beneficial and harmful people alike reach an end.
rows.anchor: فهو إدماج للتذكير بحالة الممات واستواء الناس فيها من نافع وضار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The juxtaposition of the rain parable with 39:22–23 signals the lesson drawn from it: the Qur’an-guided response parallels the growth of vegetation.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى العبرة من هذا التمثيل

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a report in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Prophet likens his guidance and knowledge to abundant rain: receptive fertile soil yields growth, water-retaining soil benefits others, and barren land accepts neither; these represent people who learn and teach, transmit benefit, or reject guidance.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the passage’s primary purpose is to prove God’s sole divinity from creation; the rain analogy to Qur’anic guidance is embedded within that proof.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون المعنى أصالة وإدماجا على عكس ما بينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On either structural reading, the passage alludes to the possibility that God will bring people to life a second time.
rows.anchor: وعلى كلا الوجهين أدمج في أثناء الكلام إيماء إلى إمكان إحياء الناس حياة ثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “People of understanding” are those who use their reason, benefit from the evidence, and believe; this implies that those who do not benefit from it are like people without minds.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا تعريض بأن الذين لم يستفيدوا من الأدلة بمنزلة من عدموا العقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question follows from the contrast with the God-fearing promised chambers in 39:20 and the preceding parable of benefiting from the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: فرع عليه هذا الاستفهام التقريري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative pronoun “whoever” is the subject, with an omitted predicate inferred from the contrast: like the one condemned to punishment in the darkness of unbelief, or like the one whose heart is hard.
rows.anchor: مما اقتضاه حرف الاستدراك من مخالفة حالة لحال من حق عليه كلمة العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Expanding the breast for Islam” metaphorically means the mind accepts and loves Islam; literal breast-opening is likened to relieving the constriction that confusion and distress produce in breathing.
rows.anchor: وشرح الصدر للإسلام استعارة لقبول العقل هدي الإسلام ومحبته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s elegant choice of “expand” captures the happiness, confidence, resilience, and freedom from doubt that Islamic teaching and character give the believer.
rows.anchor: لأن تعاليم الإسلام وأخلاقه وآدابه تكسب المسلم فرحا بحاله ومسرة برضى ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam lifts the believer above idolatry, forms wisdom, noble and sincere conduct, brotherhood, contentment, patience, hope, and gratitude; confidence in God makes him clear-sighted, brave, and dignified.
rows.anchor: فكان صدره منشرحا بالإسلام متلقيا الحوادث باستبصار غير هياب شجاع القلب عزيز النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is causal: God expanded his breast for the sake of Islam, meaning for its acceptance.
rows.anchor: واللام في { للإسلام } لام العلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “he is upon light” refers back to “whoever” whose breast God expanded.
rows.anchor: فالضمير عائد إلى { من }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Light is a metaphor for guidance and clarity of truth: it reveals things and removes darkness and confusion.
rows.anchor: مستعار للهدى ووضوح الحق لأن النور به تنجلي الأشياء ويخرج المبصر من غياهب الضلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Upon” is metaphorically used for being firmly established in light, as in 2:5.
rows.anchor: واستعيرت { على } استعارة تبعية أو تمثيلية للتمكن من النور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From his Lord” modifies “light”; min marks its origin, so this is complete divine light without darkness, like the light God guides people to in 24:35.
rows.anchor: أي نور موصوف بأنه جاء به من عند الله فهو نور كامل لا تخالطه ظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those whose breasts were not expanded have innate hard hearts through which the call to good cannot enter; “woe” summarizes their extreme misery and wretchedness.
rows.anchor: يدل على حال ضده وهم الذين لم يشرح الله صدورهم للإسلام فكانت لقلوبهم قساوة فطروا عليها فلا تسلك دعوة الخير إلى قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Woe” conveys the utmost misery and wretchedness, a sense detailed at 2:79.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم تفصيل معانيه عند قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hardness literally means thickness and solidity in bodies; hard hearts metaphorically mean minds little affected by admonitions, while softness denotes quick receptiveness.
rows.anchor: مستعارة لقلة تأثر العقل بما يسدى إلى صاحبه من المواعظ ونحوها

rows.speaker: مغني اللبيب
rows.claim: Mughni al-Labib treats min as equivalent to ʿan (“away from/about”), citing this verse and 50:22.
rows.anchor: استشهد له في مغني اللبيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAshur finds the “min means ʿan” analysis unnecessary: here min can mark cause, as al-Zamakhshari says, and in 50:22 it marks a starting point.
rows.anchor: وفيه نظر ، لإمكان حملهما على معنيين شائعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Remembrance of God” here means the Qur’an, and its attribution to God honors it.
rows.anchor: والمراد بذكر الله القرآن وإضافته إلى الله زيادة تشريف له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a Qur’anic verse is recited, the disbelievers recoil; the resulting aversion settles in them and hardens their hearts.
rows.anchor: أنهم إذا تليت آية اشمأزوا فتمكن الاشمئزاز منهم فقست قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their unbelief makes them hate the Qur’anic call to Islam; repeated avoidance and resistance entrench that hatred until their hearts become hard.
rows.anchor: فكلما سمعوه أعرضوا وعاندوا وتجددت كراهية الإسلام في قلوبهم حتى ترسخ تلك الكراهية في قلوبهم فتصير قلوبهم قاسية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same remembrance that brings believers’ hearts tranquility can harden disbelievers’ hearts because effects vary with receptivity; a sound heart softens, while obstinacy and pride deepen the disease.
rows.anchor: وسبب ذلك اختلاف القابلية فإن السبب الواحد تختلف آثاره وأفعاله باختلاف القابلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement is an explanatory resumption answering why mention of God hardens their hearts: they are so immersed in misguidance that hearing it cannot dispel their error.
rows.anchor: مستأنفة استئنافا بيانيا لأن ما قبله من الحكم بأن قساوة قلوبهم من أجل أن يذكر الله عندهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative after their hard-heartedness marks them as deserving their ensuing state; severe misguidance causes hardness and is also its consequence, as psychological causes and effects can reciprocate without temporal circularity.
rows.anchor: وافتتاح هذه الجملة باسم الإشارة عقب ما وصفوا به من قساوة القلوب لإفادة أن ما سيذكر من حالهم بعد الإشارة إليهم صاروا به أحرياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubin means intense and unmistakable; it is figurative for firmly rooted misguidance, evident to a reflective observer.
rows.anchor: فالمبين كناية عن القوة والرسوخ فهو يبين للمتأمل أنه ضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passage explains that Qur’anic guidance softens God-fearing hearts; hardness comes from inner rust, as with the sealed hearts in 2:6–7, not from any shortcoming in the Qur’an’s guidance.
rows.anchor: مبينة أن قساوة قلوب الضالين من سماع القرآن إنما هي لرين في قلوبهم وعقولهم لا لنقص في هدايته

rows.speaker: عياض
rows.claim: In al-Shifāʾ, Qadi ʿIyāḍ counts the awe and grandeur that seize listeners as an aspect of the Qur’an’s inimitability, since its elevated rank surpasses all speech.
rows.anchor: عياض في ( الشفاء ) من وجوه إعجاز القرآن : الروعة التي تلحق قلوب سامعيه

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت أبي بكر
rows.claim: Asma bint Abi Bakr reports that the Prophet’s Companions wept and their skins shivered when the Qur’an was recited to them, as described here.
rows.anchor: وعن أسماء بنت أبي بكر كان أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا قرىء عليهم القرآن كما نعتهم الله تدمع أعينهم وتقشعر جلودهم

words: تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse singles out God-fearing people for gooseflesh because it is followed by their skin and hearts softening.
rows.anchor: وخص القشعريرة بالذين يخشون ربهم باعتبار ما سيردف به

rows.speaker: عياض
rows.claim: Qadi ʿIyāḍ says the Qur’an’s awe affects deniers even more intensely, so they find hearing it burdensome and turn away, as in 17:46.
rows.anchor: قال عياض : ( وهي ، أي الروعة التي تلحق قلوب سامعيه عند سماعه ، على المكذبين به أعظم

rows.speaker: جبير بن مطعم
rows.claim: In a report the author calls authentic, Jubayr ibn Mutʿim says the Prophet’s recitation of al-Ṭūr 35–37 nearly made his heart fly; that was when Islam first took root in him.
rows.anchor: عن جبير بن مطعم قال : ( سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقرأ في المغرب بالطور

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi says he was told that ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, deeply moved by the Prophet’s Fussilat recitation and its warning, covered the Prophet’s mouth and begged him by kinship to stop; the source gives no grading.
rows.anchor: روي عن محمد بن كعب القرظي قال : ( أخبرت أن عتبة بن ربيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For believers, awe during recitation keeps drawing them toward the Qur’an and gives them delight because their hearts incline to it.
rows.anchor: وأما المؤمن فلا تزال روعته وهيبته إياه مع تلاوته توليه انجذابا وتكسبه هشاشة لميل قلبه إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling this God’s guidance means that God prepared the Qur’an’s qualities for guidance and added it to Himself because He revealed it for that purpose.
rows.anchor: راجع إلى ما هيأه الله للهدى من صفات القرآن فإضافته إليه بأنه أنزله لذلك

words: يَهْدِى بِهِۦ مَن يَشَآءُ وَمَن يُضْلِلِ ٱللَّهُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing guidance and misguidance to God describes how different audiences respond to the Qur’an, which fully supplies the means to guide.
rows.anchor: ومعنى إسناد الهدى والإضلال إلى الله راجع إلى مراتب تأثر المخاطبين بالقرآن وعدم تأثرهم بحيث كان القرآن مستوفيا لأسباب اهتداء الناس به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “that” refers to the Qur’an itself as God’s guidance or proof of it: those God wills to guide follow it, while those He wills to stray disbelieve it.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون الإشارة إلى { أحسن الحديث }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whomever He wills” elides “to guide”: God’s will creates the person’s receptivity and determines guidance; the contrasting clause implies that one not willed guidance persists in error.
rows.anchor: وهي إرادته بأنه يهتدي فخلقه متأثرا بتلك المشيئة فقدر له الاهتداء

words: وَمَن يُضْلِلِ ٱللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُۥ مِنْ هَادٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whoever God leads astray has no guide” is a conclusion to the explanatory passage.
rows.anchor: فجملة { ومن يضلل الله فما له من هاد } تذييل للاستئناف البياني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse interrupts Qur’an-praise before 39:27; commentators connect it to the two outcomes in 39:23, with an omitted comparison and a reportive or rejecting question: the punished and the blessed are not equal.
rows.anchor: وجعلها المفسرون تفريعا على جملة { ذلك هدى الله يهدي به من يشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted comparison is with one safe from punishment through God’s guidance, as in the parallel question at 47:14; the guided do not suffer the torment.
rows.anchor: والقول فيه مثل القول في سابقه من الاستفهام وحذف الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAshur’s preferred construction makes the question identify the referent of “whoever God leads astray” in 39:23: the omitted subject is “is he the one who shields his face from torment?”
rows.anchor: تفريعا لتعيين ما صدق ( من ) في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ittiqāʾ means undertaking protection, restraint, and warding off; waqā takes two objects and may mark the instrument of protection with bi.
rows.anchor: وفعلها يتعدى إلى مفعولين ، يقال : وقى نفسه ضرب السيف ، ويتعدى بالباء إلى سبب الوقاية

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse, “she protected us with her hand,” illustrates bi marking the means by which protection is achieved.
rows.anchor: وقال النابغة : سقط النصيف ولم ترد إسقاطه فتناولته واتقتنا باليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the iftiʿāl form, the verb takes one object, which was the second object of the base verb waqā.
rows.anchor: وأصله مفعول ثان إذ أصله : وقى نفسه سوء العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the face is most precious and normally shielded from blows, claiming to shield oneself with one’s face is sarcastic allusion to having no protection; compare 18:29.
rows.anchor: مستعملا كناية عن عدم الوقاية على طريقة التهكم أو التلميح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The evil of the torment” is the object of ittqā; in the base construction it is the second object of waqā, but the derived form governs one object.
rows.anchor: و { سوء العذاب } منصوب على المفعولية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And it was said” may be coordinated with the relative clause, with “whoever” understood collectively as “they”; “the wrongdoers” replaces a pronoun to imply their punishment is caused by their shirk.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون { وقيل } عطفا على الصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one with no shield against punishment is told to taste the torment.
rows.anchor: تنجيه من ذوق العذاب فيقال لهم : ذوقوا العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “the wrongdoers” broadly includes polytheists from all peoples; the sentence then sums up their common fate and leads into the denial by earlier peoples in 39:25.
rows.anchor: جميع الذين أشركوا بالله من الأمم غير خاص بالمشركين المتحدث عنهم
